{"url": "https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.20977v3.pdf", "scope": "bounded PDF text extraction from up to 24 pages; figures, tables, equations, layout, and scanned-image text may be incomplete", "excerpt": "Evaluating and Steering Modality Preferences in Multi-modal LLMs
Yu Zhang1 2 Jinlong Ma 1 Yongshuai Hou2 Xuefeng Bai 1 Kehai Chen 1 2 Yang Xiang2 Jun Yu1
Min Zhang 1 2
Abstract
Multi-modal large language models (MLLMs)
have achieved remarkable success on complex
multi-modal tasks. However, it remains
insufficiently explored whether they exhibit
modality preference, a tendency to favor one
modality over another when processing multi-
modal contexts. To study this question, we
introduceMC 2 benchmark, which constructs
controlled evidence-conflict scenarios to system-
atically evaluate modality preference in decision-
making. Extensive experiments reveal that all
20 tested MLLMs generally demonstrate clear
modality preferences, and such preferences can
serve as a useful indicator of downstream task
performance of MLLMs. Further analysis shows
that modality preference can be controlled by
instruction guidance and captured within the
latent representations of MLLMs. Built on these
insights, we propose a probing and steering
method based on representation engineering to
explicitly control modality preference without
requiring additional fine-tuning. This method
effectively amplifies modality preference toward
a desired direction and demonstrates promising
improvements across multiple multi-modal
understanding and reasoning tasks.

Autonomous robots operating in open and changing environments must adapt not only what they know, but also how they think, learn, and interact when previously unseen situations arise. However, most existing approaches assume predefined reasoning, learning, or interaction mechanisms and mainly adapt knowledge or model parameters within these fixed structures. This paper proposes an open-ended cognitive evolution framework that maintains a minimal cognitive core while allowing concrete thinking, learning, and interaction methods to be selected, validated, reused, updated, and expanded according to observed evidence and accumulated experience. The framework also incorporates discrepancy-driven evaluation to detect when previously valid knowledge or capabilities have become outdated. Experiments over five independent seeds show that newly acquired thinking activities achieve 94.67% first-encounter success on unseen conflict families, with 98.67% reuse. Adaptive learning-method selection reaches 95.00% accuracy and improves task success to 69.16%, compared with 55.66% for the best fixed learner. Under unannounced environmental changes, the proposed method achieves 96.43% task success, only 1.07% hazard rate and 1.43% outdated decisions, while reducing verification operations by 48.0% relative to periodic updating.
